A better kind of bookmark

The vocabulary bookmark for readers, writers, and thinkers. Capture new words as you read — without losing your place, focus, or flow.

Embrace an analog reading experience

How it works

01
Read

Place your Word-Mark in your book. When you meet a word you don't know, jot it down and keep reading with minimal interruption.

02
Define

At the end of your session, look up each word and write its meaning beside it. The act of writing commits it to memory.

03
Collect

Once full, bind your bookmark into your book of new words with the brass brads. Start a fresh one. Watch your vocabulary grow.

Introducing the definitive vocabulary bookmark

Anatomy of a Word-Mark

  1. 01 Bookmark title

    A gentle reminder of the linguistic discoveries that await you on every page.

  2. 02 Inspirational quote

    A different quote on every bookmark, from writers who understood the power of language.

  3. 03 Room for up to 20 definitions

    Front and back, for words and their meanings.

  4. 04 Pebbled writing surface

    Provides a beautiful tactile writing experience suitable for your new terms.

  5. 05 Binding holes

    Three pre-punched holes, so your completed bookmark slots straight into your book of new words.

  6. 06 Marginal thoughts

    A column for the ideas that don't fit elsewhere, obscured once the page is bound.

A unified system

What's inside

Each package contains five bookmarks — each one bearing a different literary quote — along with everything needed to bind them into a lasting reference.

  • 5 bookmarks, each with a unique quote 20 words each
  • 2 notes pages Lined
  • 1 cover Black, gold detail
  • 3 brass bindings Reusable
A note on materials

Each component of Word‑Mark™ has been meticulously chosen. Bookmarks and note pages are printed on 110 lb premium pebbled cardstock — a heavy-weight, eggshell-textured stock that takes ink beautifully and rewards the act of writing. The 130 lb cardstock cover is substantial enough to protect what's inside and elegant enough to earn its place on your bookshelf, with gold ink and UV spot treatment. Brass bindings are made to be assembled and reassembled as your book of new words grows. Packaging is made from PLA, a plant-based material that cuts greenhouse gases by up to 70% compared to regular plastic packaging.

About

For years, I earned a living by writing — first as an editor, then as a writer in banking and tech.

With each role and salary increase, my professional vocabulary grew more constrained, until the point where I was earning six figures designing content systems for apps, but was obliged to write to a 6th-grade level to remain accessible to an international, non-native English-speaking audience.

When I lost my job in tech, I disappeared into literature. Because why not? On average it's far less depressing than the current state of affairs. It quickly became apparent just how far I had drifted from the vibrant literary mind of my youth. The tedium of adult labour had blunted my creativity and vernacular.

As I read, I found myself repeatedly looking up words I didn't know. But the act of looking up new words on my phone disrupted my reading process. I would set my phone down half an hour later, having browsed new job postings, scrolled mindlessly, and altogether abandoned the literary world, only to realise I had forgotten to look up that word. And where was I in my book?

My phone, I decided, had no place in my reading experience.

As something of a purist, I've always favoured physical books over eReaders. The smell of aging ink on paper, decaying glue. The satisfying act of turning a page.

If you're reading this, maybe you do, too.

So I started using a scrap piece of paper as a bookmark. Each time I encountered an unfamiliar word, I would write it down on the paper and continue reading. I could always understand the sentence well enough without looking the word up right away — I could make sense of the word contextually. And writing it down demanded only the briefest interruption to my reading. Later, at the end of my reading session, I would look up the word and record its meaning.

The act of writing it down helped me commit it to memory. I soon ended up with lots of little scraps, filled with words and their meanings.

Pretty cool, I thought. I should put these together into some sort of book.

And so, the idea of Word‑Mark was born. From there, I set about designing the perfect vocabulary bookmark. And this is what I came up with.

Daniel McLeod

Founder, Word‑Mark™ · Vancouver, BC
